bullets: Queen Victoria and **Prince Albert** popularised the Christmas tree (a German custom), famously in an 1848 illustration.
The first commercial **Christmas card** was produced in 1843, the year of the novella.
Christmas became associated with **family, feasting, charity and goodwill**; Dickens’s descriptions of the Cratchits’ dinner and Fezziwig’s ball helped define this ideal.
Dickens presents Christmas as a **moral** season: Fred calls it a time when people treat those ‘below them’ as ‘fellow-passengers to the grave’.
core.p: In the early 19th century, Christmas was less important than it later became. During the 1840s it was revived and reshaped.

bullets: It could be read in **one sitting**, or aloud to a family by the fire, which suited the Christmas setting. Dickens later gave hugely popular public readings of it.
Its compact structure allowed a clear **moral fable** with a single transformation.
It borrows from the **ghost story** tradition, popular at Christmas.
The illustrated first edition (by John Leech) was beautifully produced: a gift book.
core.p: A novella is longer than a short story but shorter than a novel.

bullets: A **stave** is a verse of a song (also the lines of music). The novella is structured like a carol, a song of joy and religious celebration.
Five staves resemble the **five acts** of a play: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
The title ‘A Christmas Carol’ suggests the story should be shared, repeated and remembered like a song.

callouts.p: A strong AO2/AO3 point: calling the chapters ‘staves’ presents the book as a carol, a public celebration meant to spread its message from home to home.

core.p: Dickens divides the book into five **‘staves’** instead of chapters.

bullets: Fred says Christmas is ‘venerat[ed]’ for its ‘sacred name and origin’ but also good in itself.
Tiny Tim hopes people will remember ‘who made lame beggars walk, and blind men see’ (Jesus).
Scrooge’s transformation follows a Christian pattern of **sin, repentance and redemption**.
core.p: Victorian Britain was a Christian society, and the novella blends religious and secular Christmas.

model: Christmas as a lens on poverty (Ignorance and Want)
Context: Christmas revival, staves as carol
exam.q: Explain how Dickens presents the importance of Christmas elsewhere in the novella. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Christmas is both a setting and a moral standard.

mistakes.r: The word links the structure to a carol: explain the effect.

quotes.a: Everyone shares the same journey; equality.
Inclusive blessing; the novella’s final line.
Christmas as a moral practice all year.
quotes.q: he knew how to keep Christmas well

summary: The 1840s saw a revival of Christmas as a family festival of generosity, which Dickens helped to shape; and he chose the novella form, divided into five ‘staves’ like a carol, so that the book could be read aloud in one sitting and move its readers.

terms.d: A verse of a song; Dickens’s name for his chapters.
A story that teaches a moral lesson.
